headline: Wild Tiger Numbers Are Rising—Here's Why It Matters
meta_description: Wild tiger populations are increasing despite massive conservation challenges. Nepal has nearly tripled its tigers since 2009.
summary_short: Wild tigers are one of the few endangered species whose numbers are actually climbing. Nepal's dramatic recovery shows what's possible when conservation works.
body:
Wild tigers are one of the few major endangered species whose numbers are actually going up—a remarkable achievement given how difficult they are to protect.

Tigers demand enormous territories, intact forests, abundant prey, and constant protection from poaching. They also require something harder to guarantee: peaceful coexistence with nearby human communities. That multiple countries have managed to align all these factors simultaneously reveals the depth of their commitment to tiger conservation. India now holds the largest share with more than 3,600 tigers, while Nepal has achieved one of the most dramatic recoveries, nearly tripling its wild tiger population since 2009.

This upward trend proves that even species facing the steepest odds can recover when resources, political will, and community support converge.
quick_facts: Nepal nearly tripled its wild tiger population since 2009
India holds more than 3,600 tigers, the largest share
Tigers require intact forests, abundant prey, and anti-poaching protection
Tiger recovery requires coexistence with human communities
